issues.legal_issue: The doctrine of res judicata does not bar a later statutory tenancy application when the earlier determination was made in summary proceedings and the statute does not expressly apply that doctrine to such determinations.
material_facts: The tenants’ earlier application was rejected because they had not then completed the required period of possession, and that rejection was upheld by the authorities and the High Court.
The tenants later made another application seeking ownership rights based on their tenancy.
The tenancy authorities decided the applications summarily, without an elaborate trial, framed issues, or proceedings equivalent to a civil suit.
The statute did not expressly make the doctrine of res judicata applicable to those summary determinations.
issues.conclusion: The earlier summary determination did not operate as res judicata to bar the later application, and the High Court erred in holding otherwise.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of res judicata under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply to summary proceedings unless the statute expressly extends it to the orders made in those proceedings. The authorities were not civil courts and the applications were not plaints tried as civil suits.

rule.if: summary_tenancy_proceeding and prior_order_lacked_full_trial and later_application_seeks_tenancy_relief and statute_does_not_expressly_extend_res_judicata

predicates.summary_tenancy_proceeding: The matter was a tenancy application decided by an administrative authority in a summary proceeding.
predicates.prior_order_lacked_full_trial: The earlier determination was made without an elaborate trial equivalent to a civil suit.
predicates.later_application_seeks_tenancy_relief: The tenant later applied again for relief arising from the tenancy.
predicates.statute_does_not_expressly_extend_res_ju: The governing statute did not expressly make res judicata applicable to orders in the summary proceeding.

issues.definition: When a tenancy matter is decided summarily, the earlier order does not bar a later tenancy application if the statute does not expressly extend res judicata to such orders.

issues.legal_issue: A qualifying tenant may acquire the landlord’s proprietary rights by applying after completing the required continuous tenancy, even if that period was not completed before the governing enactment commenced.
material_facts: The tenants were tenants under the applicable general tenancy law and were in possession as tenants before the commencement of the relevant enactment.
They had completed the required continuous period of tenancy before seeking to exercise the purchase right, though they had not completed it when their earlier application was rejected.
The landlord’s application to reserve the land for personal cultivation had been rejected, and that decision had become final.
The landlord held more land than the applicable ownership limit, and the tenants’ personal cultivation did not exceed the protected limit.
The authorities allowed the later application for proprietary rights, and the compensation determined by them had been deposited.
issues.conclusion: The tenants satisfied the requirements for acquiring the proprietary rights and were entitled to purchase those rights; the appeal was allowed and the authorities’ orders were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(k), 7A, 20 and 22 of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, a tenant must fall within the applicable definition of tenant, have been in possession as a tenant when the President’s Act commenced, and complete the required continuous tenancy before exercising the purchase right. The required period need not have been completed before that commencement. The tenant must also not be liable to ejectment on the relevant additional grounds. The Court rejected the contrary temporal interpretation adopted in Jaisi Ram v. Financial Commissioner, Revenue, Punjab & Ors., AIR 1972 Punjab and Haryana 72, because it would defeat the Act’s object of conferring ownership on the tiller of the land.

rule.if: statutory_tenant_purchase_application and qualifying_tenant_status and tenant_in_possession_at_commencement and qualifying_continuous_tenancy_before_application and not ejectable_on_additional_grounds

predicates.statutory_tenant_purchase_application: The tenant applied under a statutory scheme for the right to purchase the landlord’s proprietary interest in the land held as a tenant.
predicates.qualifying_tenant_status: The applicant was a tenant within the applicable general tenancy-law definition.
predicates.tenant_in_possession_at_commencement: The applicant was in possession of the land as a tenant when the relevant enactment commenced.
predicates.qualifying_continuous_tenancy_before_app: The applicant completed the required continuous period of tenancy before applying to exercise the purchase right, even if that period was not complete at the enactment’s commencement.
predicates.ejectable_on_additional_grounds: The landlord could terminate the tenancy on the relevant additional statutory grounds.

issues.definition: A qualifying tenant in possession when the enactment commenced may acquire the proprietary rights by applying after completing the required continuous tenancy, provided the tenant is not ejectable on the relevant additional grounds.
